title: Data access: connection pooling and schema migrations
seriesDescription: Topic-by-topic JEE-style quizzes for the backend and AI-engineering interview roadmap: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code writing, plus multi-correct questions. Language core, concurrency, DSA, web frameworks, data access, databases, messaging, resilience, security, testing, system design, LLM and agent engineering.
description: HikariCP and SQLAlchemy/asyncpg pool settings, the pool-sizing formula, Little's law and pool exhaustion; Flyway, Liquibase and Alembic migrations and zero-downtime schema changes.
source: HikariCP README and wiki (About Pool Sizing, pool locking); SQLAlchemy 2.0 pooling docs; asyncpg docs; PostgreSQL docs (max_connections, superuser_reserved_connections); Flyway (Redgate), Liquibase and Alembic docs; Spring Boot reference

questions.prompt: The HikariCP "About Pool Sizing" guidance (from the PostgreSQL community) suggests connections = (core_count * 2) + effective_spindle_count as a starting point. The database server has 4 cores and its data lives on one effective spindle (a single SSD). How many connections should the pool start with?
questions.explanation: 4 * 2 + 1 = 9. The point of the formula is that a small pool is usually enough: a database cannot run more CPU-bound queries in parallel than it has cores, and the rest just queue and context switch. Treat it as a starting point and load-test.

questions.prompt: A service handles 200 requests per second at steady state and each request holds a database connection for 50 ms on average. By Little's law, how many connections are in use on average?
questions.explanation: L = lambda * W = 200 req/s * 0.05 s = 10 connections busy on average. Size above the average for bursts, but a pool of 10-20 serves 200 req/s; the mistake is to take 200 requests as 200 connections.

questions.prompt: PostgreSQL runs with max_connections = 100 and the default superuser_reserved_connections = 3. Every application pod has a HikariCP pool with maximumPoolSize = 15 and all pools can be fully busy at peak. What is the largest number of pods that cannot exhaust the usable connections?
questions.explanation: 100 - 3 = 97 usable connections; 6 pods need 90, 7 pods need 105 > 97. At that scale add PgBouncer (transaction pooling) or shrink the per-pod pool; per-instance pools multiply with every autoscaled pod.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: Raising a connection pool from 20 to 200 on the same database server often makes throughput worse, not better.
questions.reason: More simultaneously active connections than CPU cores add context switching, lock contention and cache pressure.

whys.a: Correct: R is the mechanism behind A.
whys.b: R is exactly why A holds, so it does explain it.
whys.c: R is true, so this option wrongly calls it false.
whys.d: A is true in practice, so this option wrongly calls it false.

questions.explanation: Requests wait in the pool queue instead of fighting inside the database. Add a bounded pool, short transactions and, if needed, PgBouncer rather than a bigger pool.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: Flyway applies a versioned migration such as V3__add_status.sql exactly once per database.
questions.reason: Flyway re-executes a versioned migration whenever the checksum of its file changes.

whys.a: R is false, so it cannot explain A.
whys.b: R is false, so this option wrongly calls both statements true.
whys.c: Correct: A is true; R is false because a changed checksum makes validation fail instead of re-running.
whys.d: A is true, so this option wrongly calls it false.

questions.explanation: Only repeatable migrations (R__*.sql) re-run when their checksum changes. For a versioned migration that was already applied, fix forward with a new version, or use flyway repair deliberately.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=update is a good way to manage the schema of a production database.
questions.reason: Hibernate update mode only adds missing tables and columns; it never drops or renames anything and keeps no history.

whys.a: A is false, so both-true options are wrong.
whys.b: A is false, so both-true options are wrong.
whys.c: R is true, so this option wrongly calls it false.
whys.d: Correct: A is false because you get no reviewable, repeatable, ordered scripts, no renames or data fixes and no rollback story; R is true.

questions.explanation: Use Flyway or Liquibase for production and, at most, ddl-auto=validate to check that entities match the schema.

questions.text: HikariCP's {1} defaults to 10. A thread that waits longer than {2} (30 seconds by default) for a connection gets an exception. {3} retires connections before the database or a firewall silently closes them, and {4} logs a warning with the stack trace of code that keeps a connection too long.
questions.explanation: maxLifetime should be a few seconds shorter than any server or infrastructure timeout. leakDetectionThreshold is off (0) by default; set it in staging to find code that forgets to close or holds a connection across slow calls.

questions.prompt: Match each symptom to the most appropriate first response.

left.text: SQLAlchemy: "QueuePool limit of size 5 overflow 10 reached, connection timed out"
psycopg: "server closed the connection unexpectedly" after a quiet night
PostgreSQL: "FATAL: sorry, too many clients already"
Hikari: "Connection is not available, request timed out after 30000ms"

right.text: Return connections sooner: close sessions, shorten transactions, no slow I/O inside them
Enable pool_pre_ping or a pool_recycle shorter than the server or firewall idle timeout
Cap per-instance pool sizes or put PgBouncer in front of the database
Set leakDetectionThreshold to log where connections are being held

questions.explanation: Exhaustion (wait for a free connection) and stale connections (dead sockets in the pool) look different but both show up as pool errors. Raising max_connections just moves the memory cost to the database.

questions.prompt: Create the SQLAlchemy engine `engine` for the URL in DATABASE_URL with a pool of 10 connections, at most 5 extra overflow connections, a 10 second wait for a free connection, and a liveness check on checkout.
questions.model:
engine = create_engine(
    DATABASE_URL, pool_size=10, max_overflow=5,
    pool_timeout=10, pool_pre_ping=True)
questions.explanation: Defaults of the QueuePool are pool_size=5, max_overflow=10, pool_timeout=30. The hard cap per process is pool_size + max_overflow; remember to multiply by the number of processes.

questions.prompt: Write the Spring Boot application.yml fragment that configures the Hikari pool with a maximum of 10 connections, a 3000 ms connection timeout and leak detection after 20000 ms.
questions.model:
spring:
  datasource:
    hikari:
      maximum-pool-size: 10
      connection-timeout: 3000
      leak-detection-threshold: 20000
questions.explanation: Spring Boot relaxed binding accepts maximumPoolSize or maximum-pool-size. A short connection timeout makes overload fail fast instead of piling up threads.

questions.prompt: Using asyncpg and a DSN string `dsn`, create a pool with a minimum of 2 and a maximum of 10 connections, then acquire a connection from it and read the number of rows in table orders into `n`.

checks.label: acquires a connection with async with pool.acquire()
awaits a query such as fetchval

questions.model:
pool = await asyncpg.create_pool(dsn, min_size=2, max_size=10)
async with pool.acquire() as conn:
    n = await conn.fetchval("SELECT count(*) FROM orders")
questions.explanation: Create the pool once at application start (for example in a FastAPI lifespan handler), not per request. asyncpg placeholders are $1, $2, and the default pool is min_size=10, max_size=10.

questions.prompt: A developer edits V3__add_status.sql after it already ran on staging, then deploys. What does Flyway do on staging at startup?

options.text: Validation fails on a checksum mismatch and the application refuses to start.
options.why: Right: Flyway stores a checksum for each applied migration and validates it on migrate.

options.text: It silently re-runs V3 and applies the new SQL.
options.why: Versioned migrations are never re-run automatically.

options.text: It computes the difference to the stored script and applies only the new lines to the table.
options.why: Flyway has no concept of diffing a script.

options.text: It ignores the change because V3 is already in flyway_schema_history.
options.why: It does not ignore it: the stored checksum no longer matches.

questions.explanation: Rule of the trade: applied migrations are immutable; add V4 to correct course. flyway repair realigns checksums only when you know the database really has the intended state.

questions.prompt: Match each description to the Flyway, Liquibase or Alembic artifact.
questions.explanation: Liquibase identifies a changeset by id + author + file path and records it in DATABASECHANGELOG; Flyway orders by version and records checksums in flyway_schema_history; Alembic stores only the current revision id in alembic_version.

questions.prompt: Write the two shell commands that generate an Alembic revision named "add status" by comparing the models with the database, and then apply all pending revisions.

checks.label: gives the revision a message with -m
applies migrations with alembic upgrade head

questions.model:
alembic revision --autogenerate -m "add status"
alembic upgrade head
questions.explanation: Always read the generated script: autogenerate cannot detect column renames (it emits drop + add), many constraint changes or data migrations. alembic downgrade -1 steps back one revision.

questions.prompt: Select all practices that make a schema change safer for a zero-downtime deployment on PostgreSQL.

options.text: Add the new column as nullable, backfill in batches, then add the NOT NULL constraint in a later release.
options.why: Right: avoids long locks and works with old and new code.

options.text: Use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY on a large live table (outside a transaction block).
options.why: Right: it avoids blocking writes, at the cost of a slower build.

options.text: Use expand/contract: ship code that works with both schemas before dropping the old column.
options.why: Right: old and new application versions run side by side during a rolling deploy.

options.text: Rename a column in one step while old and new application versions are both running.
options.why: The old version immediately fails because its column no longer exists.

options.text: Edit the already-applied migration file to include the extra change.
options.why: Applied migrations are immutable; the change would never reach databases that already ran it.

questions.explanation: Think in two phases per breaking change: expand (additive, compatible) then contract (cleanup after all code uses the new shape).

questions.prompt: Each request thread holds one connection and, through nested REQUIRES_NEW calls, needs 4 connections at the same time. There are 5 such threads. Using the HikariCP pool-locking rule (threads x (connections needed per thread - 1) + 1), what is the smallest pool size that can never deadlock?
questions.explanation: 5 x (4 - 1) + 1 = 16. With fewer, all 5 threads can each grab some connections and wait forever for the rest. The better cure is to avoid holding a connection while asking for another (no REQUIRES_NEW inside open transactions).

questions.prompt: A Spring Boot service sets spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size=20 and leaves minimum-idle unset. How many connections does Hikari keep in the pool while the service is idle?
questions.explanation: minimumIdle defaults to the value of maximumPoolSize, so Hikari runs a fixed-size pool of 20 and keeps all of them open. Set minimumIdle lower only if you accept the connect latency on a burst; the project recommends the default.
